# Galaxies

From a dark site, a faint glowing band arches across the whole sky. Predict
first: what is it? A cloud high in our atmosphere? Dust from the early solar
system? Part of another galaxy? Our own galaxy, seen from inside? Pick one.

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

- describe the Milky Way's structure and where the Sun is in it;
- classify galaxies by shape and connect shape to stars and gas;
- explain how rotation curves reveal dark matter.

## Our Galaxy {#the-milky-way}

The band is our own galaxy, the **Milky Way**, seen from inside. The galaxy is
a flat **disk** of stars, gas and dust about 100,000 light-years across, with a
thicker central **bulge** of older stars and a faint, roughly spherical
**halo** of old stars and globular clusters around it all. It holds a few
hundred billion stars.

We live inside the disk, so looking along it we see stars piled up in every
direction, and looking above or below it we see far fewer. Standing in a
forest you see trees all around the horizon and open sky overhead. That is the
view from inside a disk, and it is why the Milky Way is a band.

The Sun sits in the disk about 26,000 light-years (8 kiloparsecs) from the
center, which lies toward the constellation Sagittarius, hidden behind dust in
visible light. The Sun orbits the center at about 230 km/s and takes about
230 million years to go around once. Early astronomers counted stars and
concluded we were near the center; the dust had fooled them. The globular
clusters, scattered above and below the dusty disk, gave the game away: they
are centered on a point far off in Sagittarius.

## Spirals, Ellipticals, Irregulars {#galaxy-types}

The faint "spiral nebulae" of early telescopes turned out to be whole
galaxies. The nearest big one, the **Andromeda galaxy**, is about 2.5 million
light-years away, and you can see it without a telescope from a dark site.
The observable universe holds hundreds of billions of galaxies, in three
broad shapes:

| Type | Shape | Stars and gas | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Spiral** | flat disk with arms and a bulge, sometimes a bar | gas and dust; young blue stars in the arms | the Milky Way, Andromeda |
| **Elliptical** | smooth round or oval ball | old reddish stars; little gas | giant ellipticals in clusters |
| **Irregular** | no clear shape | often gas-rich, forming many stars | the Magellanic Clouds |

Color tells age. Massive blue stars live only millions of years, so blue light
means stars formed recently, and that needs gas. No gas, no new stars, which is
why ellipticals look yellow-red.

## Rotation Curves {#dark-matter}

In the solar system almost all the mass is in the Sun, so the farther out a
planet is, the weaker the pull and the slower its orbit. Mercury moves at about
47 km/s; Neptune at about 5 km/s.

A **rotation curve** plots orbital speed against distance from the center. If
a galaxy's mass were where its stars are, mostly near the center, speeds far
out would fall off the same way. Measurements of hydrogen gas, using its radio
glow, show something else: the speeds stay roughly **flat** out to the edge of
the visible disk and beyond.

Swing a ball on a string. To swing it faster at the same radius, you have to
pull harder. An orbit's speed tells you how hard gravity pulls, and the pull
tells you how much mass is inside the orbit. Fast orbits far out mean much
more mass than we can see. We call it **dark matter**. It neither emits nor
absorbs light; we detect it only through its gravity. There is about five
times as much of it as ordinary matter, in a large halo around each galaxy.

::: {.callout-important title="Known and unknown"}
That dark matter is there is well supported: rotation curves, galaxy clusters
and the bending of light all agree. What it is remains open. It is not dark gas
or dust, which we would detect, and there are too few dim stars and black holes
to account for it. Most astronomers suspect a particle no one has detected yet.
:::

## Self-check

```{=html}
<div class="quiz" data-answer="c">
  <div class="question">1. Why does the Milky Way look like a band across the sky?</div>
  <ul>
    <li data-choice="a"><label><strong>a.</strong> It is a cloud of gas in our atmosphere</label></li>
    <li data-choice="b"><label><strong>b.</strong> We are at the exact center of a sphere of stars</label></li>
    <li data-choice="c"><label><strong>c.</strong> We are inside a flat disk and see it edge-on</label></li>
    <li data-choice="d"><label><strong>d.</strong> It is a spiral arm of the Andromeda galaxy</label></li>
  </ul>
  <div class="explain">
    <strong>c</strong>. Looking along the disk we see many stars; above and below it, few. Inside the forest.
  </div>
</div>

<div class="quiz" data-answer="a">
  <div class="question">2. Stars far from a galaxy's center orbit about as fast as stars partway out. What does that imply?</div>
  <ul>
    <li data-choice="a"><label><strong>a.</strong> There is much more mass than the visible stars and gas</label></li>
    <li data-choice="b"><label><strong>b.</strong> The outer stars are younger</label></li>
    <li data-choice="c"><label><strong>c.</strong> Gravity is weaker in galaxies</label></li>
    <li data-choice="d"><label><strong>d.</strong> Most of the mass is at the center</label></li>
  </ul>
  <div class="explain">
    <strong>a</strong>. If the mass were concentrated near the center, outer speeds would fall off, as the planets' do. Flat curves mean unseen mass: dark matter.
  </div>
</div>
```

## Where this fits

Galaxies are the markers we use to measure the universe itself. In the last
chapter, their light tells us the universe is expanding.
